name: Progressive Metal
about: Progressive metal took shape in the mid-1980s when American bands raised on Rush, Yes and Iron Maiden began writing metal with the ambitions of 1970s prog: odd meters, suites, concept albums and a premium on technique. Queensrÿche and Fates Warning supplied the early classics, Watchtower and Voivod the angular extremes, and Dream Theater's Images and Words in 1992 fixed the template of virtuoso playing, keyboards and operatic tenor vocals that still defines the mainstream of the style. From the mid-1990s it absorbed death metal (Cynic, Opeth), Meshuggah's polyrhythms and Tool's hypnotic minimalism, and in the 2000s Mastodon and Between the Buried and Me brought it to a wider rock audience. It remains metal's most musicianly branch, prized by players and derided by punks in roughly equal measure.

artists.name: Dream Theater
artists.why: wrote the template on Images and Words

artists.name: Fates Warning
artists.why: the first great American prog-metal band

artists.name: Watchtower
artists.why: Texan technicians, years ahead of everyone

artists.name: Meshuggah
artists.why: polyrhythm as a way of life

artists.name: Mastodon
artists.why: took prog metal to the festivals

artists.name: Haken
artists.why: the leading British band of the 2010s

albums.title: Operation: Mindcrime
albums.why: A political rock opera with hooks, strings and Geoff Tate's soaring tenor, and the concept album that gave progressive metal its first masterpiece.

albums.title: Images and Words
albums.why: Pull Me Under got on MTV, but the whole record defined the style: Petrucci and Portnoy's virtuosity, Moore's keyboards and LaBrie's high, clean voice.

albums.title: Blackwater Park
albums.why: Steven Wilson's production brought Mikael Åkerfeldt's acoustic passages and death growls into perfect balance on the record that made Opeth a major band.

albums.title: Awaken the Guardian
albums.why: John Arch's keening vocals and Jim Matheos's winding riffs over fantasy lyrics, the point where American power metal turned into something stranger.

albums.title: Rage for Order
albums.why: Synthesizers, cold production and paranoid lyrics made the Seattle band's second album a bold, slightly ahead-of-its-time precursor to Mindcrime.

albums.title: Nothingface
albums.why: Piggy's dissonant chords and a Pink Floyd cover took the Quebec thrashers fully into progressive territory and briefly onto MTV.

albums.title: Control and Resistance
albums.why: Absurdly technical thrash with jazz-schooled rhythms, a cult record that anticipated the next two decades of technical metal.

albums.title: Parallels
albums.why: Ray Alder's warmer voice and tighter, more melodic songs made this the band's most accessible album without surrendering the odd meters.

albums.title: Focus
albums.why: Death metal, fusion, vocoder and fretless bass in one slim, startling album, ignored on release and now treated as scripture.

albums.title: Destroy Erase Improve
albums.why: The Swedes' polyrhythmic machinery arrived fully formed, with Fredrik Thordendal's fusion solos cutting through the mathematics.

albums.title: Metropolis Pt. 2: Scenes from a Memory
albums.why: A murder-mystery concept album that gave the band's technical excess a narrative to serve, widely held as their finest hour.

albums.title: Still Life
albums.why: A story of exile and revenge told across an hour of intricate, acoustic-laced death metal, the band's first truly cohesive album.

albums.title: Lateralus
albums.why: Fibonacci-sequenced vocals and Danny Carey's drumming push Tool's hypnotic alt-metal into full progressive territory, and it sold millions anyway.

albums.title: The Divine Wings of Tragedy
albums.why: Michael Romeo's neoclassical shredding and Russell Allen's power-metal voice meet on a twenty-minute title suite that justifies its length.

albums.title: Ocean Machine: Biomech
albums.why: Townsend's wall-of-sound production and emotional range made his first solo record a cult classic beyond its mixed initial reception.

albums.title: Remedy Lane
albums.why: Daniel Gildenlöw's semi-autobiographical concept album about love and loss is theatrical and overwrought in all the ways its fans adore.

albums.title: Gretchen Goes to Nebraska
albums.why: Beatles harmonies over dropped-tuning grooves, a soulful and spiritual record that influenced far more bands than it sold copies to.

albums.title: From Mars to Sirius
albums.why: The French band's environmental concept album welded groove, death metal and whale-sized riffs into their breakthrough.

albums.title: Colors
albums.why: A continuous hour that lurches between death metal, bluegrass, polka and prog balladry, somehow holding together.

albums.title: Crack the Skye
albums.why: Brendan O'Brien's production and a story about Rasputin and astral travel turned the Atlanta band's sludge into true progressive rock.

albums.title: A Social Grace
albums.why: The San Diego band's psychedelic, flute-touched debut is a cult favorite from the style's first wave, odd and endearing.

albums.title: The Mountain
albums.why: Gentle Giant counterpoint and modern heaviness on a concept album that announced the London band as the decade's best new prog-metal act.

albums.title: Coal
albums.why: Einar Solberg's falsetto and the Norwegians' staccato riffing produce a darker, more claustrophobic album than their earlier records.

albums.title: Terminal Redux
albums.why: A science-fiction thrash opera with choirs and seventy minutes of hyperspeed riffing, the most ambitious progressive thrash record in decades.
